opus-5.5.text:
I think test-time compute is one of the most important directions right now, but how people usually talk about it is a bit narrow. When people say "scaling test-time compute," they often mean making the chain of thought longer, letting the model think for more tokens before answering. That's real, and we've seen it work very well on math and coding. But the more interesting question is: what is the model actually doing with that compute, and what is it interacting with?

If the model is only thinking inside its own head, you eventually hit diminishing returns. You can reflect, backtrack, and try different approaches, but you're limited by what you already know. The bigger opportunity is when test-time compute goes into interacting with an environment: running code, searching, using tools, trying something, getting feedback, and adjusting. Then it isn't just longer thinking. It's closer to how a person actually solves a hard problem over hours or days. That's why I think agents and test-time compute are really the same story.

So I see a few dimensions. One is depth: longer reasoning on a single problem. Another is time horizon: can a system work coherently on a task for an hour, a day, a week, keeping context and memory and not drifting? I think this is where a lot of the bottleneck is now. It's less about raw intelligence and more about long-term memory, managing context, and knowing what to do next when there's no clear instruction. The third dimension is breadth: running many attempts in parallel, or many agents collaborating, and then verifying or aggregating.

Verification connects all of these. Test-time compute scales nicely where you can check the answer, like math with a ground truth or code with unit tests. For many real-world tasks, it's unclear what "correct" means, and the reward is fuzzy or delayed. So a lot of the future depends on whether we can build good environments and good evaluation signals for the messy, real tasks people care about. In some sense, I think the field is moving from "how do we train a better model" to "how do we define the right tasks and evaluations." What you measure determines what gets scaled.

And then there's the practical side: cost and utility. Spending a thousand times more compute on a question only makes sense if the answer is worth it. So I think we'll see a split. For everyday interactions, you want fast and cheap. For high-value work like research, engineering, or scientific discovery, it can make sense to let a system run for a very long time. The interesting future is when a model can decide for itself how much to think, when to ask for help, and when to stop.

So overall, I'm very optimistic, but I'd frame it as scaling not just thinking but acting and learning at test time. The ultimate version is a system that keeps getting better while it's doing the work, learning from its own experience in context. That's still very open, and I think it's one of the most exciting problems right now.

r001.rationale: The response identifies time horizon as a scaling dimension and says it requires long-term memory, clearly linking memory to scaling test-time compute.

r002.rationale: It identifies breadth as a scaling dimension, including running many attempts in parallel and having many agents collaborate.

r003.rationale: It discusses cost, utility, and choosing how long to think, but does not identify allocating compute across the different scaling dimensions for a particular application as an open question.

fable-5.1.text:
I think test-time compute is actually the more interesting half of the story right now, and the reason is pretty simple: pretraining scaling buys you a better prior, but test-time scaling buys you better search. And for a lot of the problems we actually care about, search is where the leverage is.

Let me put it in terms I've been thinking about since the ReAct and Tree of Thoughts days. A language model, at inference, is making a sequence of decisions. If you only sample once, greedily, you're trusting the prior completely. The moment you let the model think longer, generate multiple candidates, backtrack, verify, you've turned a single forward pass into a search process, and search is something we've known how to scale for decades. AlphaGo is the obvious example. Policy plus value plus more rollouts beats a bigger policy alone.

What changed with the o1-style reasoning models is that the search got internalized. Instead of me as a researcher hand-designing a tree structure, the model learns through RL when to branch, when to double-check, when to give up on a line of thought. That's a big deal, because the structure is now learned rather than engineered, and learned structure generalizes better.

So where does it go from here? A few things I'd bet on.

First, the unit of test-time compute moves from "tokens of thinking" to "actions in an environment." Right now most of the scaling curves are measured on math and code, where verification is cheap and the episode is short. The next step is long-horizon agents, where thinking longer means running more tool calls, more experiments, more browsing, and the compute is spent interacting with the world rather than just monologuing. That's where I think the real economic value is, and it's also much harder, because the feedback is sparse and slow.

Second, I think we underestimate how much the bottleneck shifts to evaluation. If you want to spend ten thousand times more compute at test time, you need some signal to tell you which of your ten thousand attempts was good. For math you have a ground truth. For "write me a research paper" or "fix this production bug" you often don't. So a lot of the progress in test-time scaling will actually be progress in verifiers, reward models, and self-evaluation. In a sense, the model's ability to judge its own work becomes the ceiling on how useful extra compute is.

Third, there's a cost dimension that people in academia sometimes ignore. If solving one problem costs a thousand dollars in inference, it doesn't matter that it's "solvable." So the engineering of adaptive compute, knowing when a problem is easy and answering fast, and when it's hard and thinking deeply, matters as much as the raw capability. Humans do this naturally. Models are just starting to.

And honestly, I think the two scaling axes aren't really separate. A lot of what you discover at test time with heavy search can be distilled back into the weights, which raises the prior, which makes the next round of search more efficient. That loop, search, distill, search again, is in my view the actual engine. It's not pretraining versus test-time. It's a flywheel between the two.

So the short version: test-time scaling has a long way to go, but the frontier is going to look less like "think for an hour about a math problem" and more like "work for a week on a task, with the judgment to know whether you're making progress." That second part, the judgment, is the hard problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses longer interactions and tool use, but does not suggest long-term memory as a new dimension for scaling test-time compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention multi-agent systems as a scaling dimension.

r003.rationale: It discusses adaptive compute and the cost of deciding when to think longer, but does not identify how to allocate compute across scaling dimensions for a particular application as an open question.

astra-6.text:
I think the important question is: what can a model actually do with more time? If it just produces a longer answer, that’s not necessarily useful. We want additional computation to translate into better decisions—by exploring alternatives, checking assumptions, or interacting with an environment.

For problems where you can verify the result, the path is relatively clear. You can try different solutions, test them, and spend more effort on the promising ones. But for an open-ended task, deciding whether you’re making progress can be as difficult as generating the answer. So scaling test-time compute also requires better evaluation and better ways of learning from feedback.

I’m particularly interested in this in the context of agents. An agent can spend extra time gathering information, running an experiment, or revising a plan based on what happens. That makes the computation more useful because it’s connected to something outside the model’s own reasoning.

And ultimately, you want that allocation to be adaptive. A simple question should get a quick answer. A difficult task might deserve minutes or hours of work. The goal isn’t to make everything think longer; it’s to learn when additional effort is worth it and how to spend it.

r002.rationale: The response discusses agents generally, but does not suggest multi-agent systems as a dimension for scaling test-time compute.

r003.rationale: It says effort should be allocated adaptively by task difficulty, but does not identify allocating compute across scaling dimensions for a particular application as an open question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what we’re scaling at test time. You can generate more candidates and select among them, spend longer reasoning through a problem, or let an agent interact with an environment—run code, inspect the result, and revise its approach. Those are different ways of turning additional compute into better answers.

The important ingredient is feedback. If you can reliably check whether a solution works, extra computation can be very useful. If you can’t, a model may spend more time elaborating on a mistaken assumption. So I wouldn’t expect simply making every response longer to be the end state.

I’m particularly interested in the agent setting, where computation buys you more opportunities to act and learn from the results. The challenge becomes deciding what to try next, what information to gather, and when to stop. That also means training and test-time compute are closely connected: we need to train models to use that additional time productively.

Ultimately, I think systems will allocate compute much more adaptively. A simple question should get a quick answer. A difficult task might justify a much longer process, provided the system can tell whether it’s making progress.
